questions.question_text: Which algebraic operation on $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$ correctly derives $1+\tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta$?

options.text: Divide every term of $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$ by $\cos^{2}\theta$, assuming $\cos\theta\neq 0$.
Divide every term of $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$ by $\sin^{2}\theta$, assuming $\sin\theta\neq 0$.
options.why: Dividing by $\sin^2\theta$ yields $1+\cot^2\theta=\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$, not the tangent-secant identity.

options.text: Take the square root of both sides of $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$.
options.why: Taking the square root gives $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta}=1$, which does not simplify to $\cos\theta+\sin\theta$ or introduce tangent.
Multiplying by $\tan^2\theta$ produces $\sin^2\theta+\tan^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\tan^2\theta$, not the standard secant identity.

questions.question_text: Which algebraic step correctly begins proving $\dfrac{1-\sin x}{\cos^{2}x} = \dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$?

options.text: Replace $\cos^{2}x$ with $1-\sin^{2}x$, then factorise the denominator as $(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)$.
Multiply both sides by $(1+\sin x)$ to clear the denominator.
options.why: Applies operations to both sides of the identity rather than working on the LHS alone.

options.text: Cancel $1-\sin x$ with $\cos^2 x$ by treating $\cos^2 x$ as $1-\sin x$.
options.why: Canceling terms without proper algebraic factoring is mathematically invalid.

options.text: Substitute $\cos^2 x = 1+\sin^2 x$ in the denominator.
options.why: Used the incorrect sign in the Pythagorean rearrangement for $\cos^2 x$.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{LHS} = \dfrac{1-\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}$
$= \dfrac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin^{2}x}$
$= \dfrac{1-\sin x}{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}$
$= \dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$
$= \text{RHS}$

questions.solution_text: Using $\sec^2(\theta)=1+\tan^2(\theta)$, subtracting $1$ from both sides gives $\sec^2(\theta)-1=\tan^2(\theta)$.
